category_descriptions.Empirical Human-Participant Data: Data collected directly from people, such as interviews, surveys, questionnaires, user studies, logs of participant interactions, task performance, or other human-subject responses.
category_descriptions.System/Artifact Evaluation Data: Data centered on evaluating a system, interface, prototype, or model output, including screenshots, inspection findings, heuristic evaluations, benchmark inputs, generated outputs, or comparison artifacts used for assessment.
category_descriptions.Literature/Corpus Review Data: Paper collections, bibliographic corpora, review samples, extracted records, or other text corpora assembled from prior publications for review, mapping, analysis, or meta-study purposes.
category_descriptions.Synthetic or Model-Generated Data: Data produced by LLMs, generative models, simulations, or other artificial generation processes, including synthetic responses, proto-personas, generated stories, or model-created interview-like outputs.
category_descriptions.No New Dataset / Conceptual Review: Papers that do not introduce or use a distinct empirical dataset in the paper itself, such as conceptual articles, position papers, or reviews that only discuss prior work or examples.

sample_values: {'datasets_used': 'Curated prompts created by students and lecturer-suggested prompts for ChatGPT; simulated interview outputs used to create proto-personas and empathy maps; student-defined user groups and question sets.', 'methods': 'UX workshop intervention in an Electronic Health Record course with 12 undergraduate engineering students; students defined healthcare user groups, formulated interview questions, and iteratively used ChatGPT to simulate patient/clinician responses; simulated interviews were synthesized into proto-personas and empathy maps and discussed in class.', 'key_findings': 'LLMs were useful as a support tool when real users were unavailable, helping students think more critically, spark empathy, identify gaps in understanding, and produce clearer links between UX research and design outcomes. The paper emphasizes that LLM outputs are hypothetical scaffolding and not a substitute for real user research.', 'evaluation_metrics': '', 'hci_context': 'UX education and early-stage healthcare design, specifically a workshop-based UX activity in an Electronic Health Record course where students practiced human-centered design methods without access to real patients or healthcare professionals.', 'llm_role': 'Conversational tool and generative user simulator to emulate patient or clinician perspectives for early UX research and ideation.', 'participants_or_users': '12 undergraduate engineering students at the University of Western Macedonia; hypothetical users included patients such as cancer patients undergoing screening and healthcare professionals.', 'comparison_baseline': 'Comparison with the previous year’s workshop without this LLM-supported approach; no formal control condition.', 'study_type': 'Short communication / workshop-based pilot study', 'relevance_judgment': True}

{'datasets_used': 'Not explicitly stated in the accessible abstract/record; likely included patient rehabilitation/outpatient data and expert input, but the source only clearly confirms patients, rehabilitation outpatient staff, pain specialists, and physical therapists supported development/validation.', 'methods': 'Methodological study to develop the Chronic Musculoskeletal Pain–E-history Acquisition System (CMP-EAS), a ChatGPT-assisted structured pain history-taking workflow integrating SOCRATES and QISS TAPED, followed by preliminary psychometric evaluation.', 'key_findings': 'The paper reports development and preliminary psychometric validation of a ChatGPT-assisted pain history-taking system for musculoskeletal rehabilitation; the accessible source does not provide detailed numeric outcomes or psychometric coefficients.', 'evaluation_metrics': 'Psychometric validation is mentioned, but the accessible source does not specify the exact metrics used.', 'hci_context': 'ChatGPT-assisted pain history-taking for musculoskeletal rehabilitation / chronic musculoskeletal pain assessment in a rehabilitation outpatient setting.', 'llm_role': 'Conversational agent that helps structure and conduct pain history-taking through a standardized question-and-answer workflow.', 'participants_or_users': 'Patients, rehabilitation outpatient staff, pain specialists, and physical therapists.', 'comparison_baseline': 'No explicit comparison baseline is stated in the accessible source.', 'study_type': 'Development and preliminary psychometric validation study.', 'relevance_judgment': 'True', 'source_urls': ['https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2468781226001104', 'https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S2468781226001104'], 'confidence': 'medium'}

{'datasets_used': 'A previously published heuristic evaluation dataset from three human experts on the P3M6 web-based system (66 identified issues); 20 screenshots from the P3M6 interface used as input to GPT-4o; a literature-grounded prompt based on Nielsen’s 10 heuristics; pilot test screenshots (2 screenshots) used to refine the prompt.', 'methods': 'Comparative study using a mixed-methods approach. Human experts’ prior heuristic evaluation of the P3M6 web system was compared with GPT-4o’s screenshot-based heuristic evaluation using Nielsen’s 10 heuristics. GPT-4o was prompted one-shot per screenshot via OpenAI Playground. Researchers consolidated GPT-4o outputs by removing duplicates and classifying false positives, then conducted descriptive analysis, Pearson’s chi-square test for issue agreement, Mann-Whitney U test for severity comparison, and thematic analysis for issues found only by GPT-4o and false positives.', 'key_findings': 'GPT-4o identified 111 issues across 20 screenshots, but after consolidation only 41 remained; 24.3% of non-duplicate issues were false positives. Only 21.2% of the issues found by human experts were also found by GPT-4o. GPT-4o performed better on heuristics related to match between system and real world and aesthetic/minimalist design, but struggled more with user control/freedom, flexibility/efficiency, and help/documentation. GPT-4o and experts did not differ significantly in severity ratings. GPT-4o often generated false positives due to hallucination or by predicting interaction issues from static screenshots. The paper concludes GPT-4o should complement, not replace, human experts.', 'evaluation_metrics': 'Issue overlap/agreement rate (21.2% shared issues); number of issues identified (111 total, 41 consolidated, 27 false positives); percentage of false positives (24.3%); issue counts by heuristic; severity levels (1–4); Pearson’s chi-square test (χ2(1)=34.1, p<.001); Mann-Whitney U test (U(NExperts=66, NGPT-4o=41)=11.7, p=.205); descriptive statistics (mean=5.55, SD=1.14).', 'hci_context': 'Heuristic evaluation of a web-based system (P3M6), a public platform for mineral research and production information, using screenshots of the interface.', 'llm_role': 'Automated heuristic evaluator / usability issue identifier from screenshots, using Nielsen’s heuristics and generating CSV-formatted issue reports.', 'participants_or_users': 'Three human HCI experts in the prior study; four HCI researchers in this study for consolidation and validation of GPT-4o outputs.', 'comparison_baseline': 'Human experts’ heuristic evaluation of the same P3M6 system.', 'study_type': 'Comparative evaluation study', 'relevance_judgment': True}

{'datasets_used': 'CHI 2023 proceedings: 879 full research papers from the ACM Digital Library, manually downloaded and text-extracted; preprocessed corpus of 879 documents; 45-paper random sample for human evaluation; extracted challenge statements (34,638 GPT-3.5 outputs and 4,392 GPT-4-selected challenges); HCI grand challenges from Shneiderman et al. (2016) and Stephanidis et al. (2019); United Nations Sustainable Development Goals labels.', 'methods': 'Two-step LLM-based insight mining pipeline: GPT-3.5 first extracted candidate research challenges from each CHI paper, then GPT-4 deduplicated and selected the five most important challenges per paper based on relevance, future impact, and novelty. Papers were text-extracted, cleaned, lowercased, and split into sentence batches for API querying with temperature set to zero. Extracted challenges were then embedded, clustered with BERTopic, and visualized interactively with UMAP/Vega-Altair. Evaluation combined quantitative text-similarity metrics and a task-specific human review of a 45-paper sample.', 'key_findings': 'The pipeline extracted 4,392 research challenges across 113 topics from the 879 CHI papers. The challenges aligned strongly with established HCI grand challenges in areas such as ethics, privacy, accessibility, and well-being, but revealed gaps in areas like human-AI collaboration and some sustainability-related concerns. Human raters judged the extracted statements to be plausible research challenges with near-perfect agreement (κ=0.97), and the approach was cost-effective at about US$50 for the full corpus. The authors conclude that LLMs can support large-scale qualitative analysis and research idea prototyping.', 'evaluation_metrics': 'Cohen’s kappa (κ=0.97 for plausibility; κ=0.86 for alignment with human-identified challenges), mean full-alignment rate 64.8%, noise rate 0.9% in GPT-3.5 outputs, mean cosine distance d=0.075 (SD=0.066) for Step 1, 98.6% verbatim reproduction in Step 2, and NLP metrics including Exact Match, Edit Distance, Word Error Rate, BLEU, ROUGE-1, ROUGE-L, METEOR, BLANC, BERTScore, and BLEURT-20. Topic coherence was also compared using silhouette scores (Sentence-BERT 0.27, text-embedding-ada-002 0.19, CLIP 0.24).', 'hci_context': 'Mining current research challenges in Human-Computer Interaction by analyzing the 2023 ACM CHI conference proceedings and comparing the extracted challenges with HCI grand challenges and the UN SDGs; also presented as an interactive visualization for exploring the HCI research landscape.', 'llm_role': 'LLMs were used as insight-mining tools: GPT-3.5 extracted candidate HCI research challenges from paper text, GPT-4 filtered and ranked them, and GPT-3.5 was also used for automatic topic labeling during iterative topic-model tuning.', 'participants_or_users': 'Two human evaluators/researchers, including a Postdoctoral Researcher with six years of HCI experience, independently reviewed a random sample of 45 papers for validation.', 'comparison_baseline': 'No dedicated algorithmic baseline for the extraction task; comparisons were made against human-identified challenges from the 45-paper sample and against established HCI grand challenges and UN SDGs. For topic modeling, Sentence-BERT, OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002, and CLIP embeddings were compared.', 'study_type': 'System paper with task-specific evaluation and human validation; mixed-methods evaluation study of an LLM-based text analysis pipeline.', 'relevance_judgment': 'True'}

{'datasets_used': 'The rapid review screened 272 records from Web of Science (including ACM Digital Library and IEEE Xplore) and included 58 reports covering 64 studies. The review also used extracted study metadata and a publicly available open dataset of the included studies (https://bit.ly/chatgptuxrr).', 'methods': 'Rapid review conducted in December 2024 following Cochrane rapid review guidance and PRISMA 2020/PRISMA-RR interim guidance. The author preregistered the protocol, searched Web of Science with a ChatGPT/UX query, screened titles/abstracts/full texts, extracted study characteristics and IV/DV data, calculated descriptive statistics, and used reflexive thematic analysis to develop frameworks for independent and dependent variables.', 'key_findings': 'ChatGPT UX measurement research is still nascent and highly diverse. Most studies used self-report measures, with fewer objective metrics or observations; validated instruments were used in only about one-quarter of studies, and many measures were novel or single-item. Commonly studied themes included usability, trust, acceptance, affect, anthropomorphism, helpfulness, and personalization. The review concludes that standardization, better validation, and broader coverage of contexts and modalities—especially voice—are needed.', 'evaluation_metrics': 'Counts and percentages of studies/variables/measures; descriptive statistics; response formats such as 7-point and 5-point Likert scales, counts/numeric data, semantic differential scales, yes/no questions, and checklists; validation and reliability checks; subjective self-reports, objective metrics, and observations. No physiological measures were reported.', 'hci_context': 'Measuring user experience of ChatGPT and similar LLM-based chatbots in HCI across contexts such as general use, education, marketing/business, medical, research, entertainment, driving, and assembly-line work; also chatbot UI, custom chatbots, robots, and virtual characters.', 'llm_role': 'ChatGPT is the LLM-based system whose user experience is being reviewed and measured; it functions as a chatbot/conversational agent, sometimes embedded in other interfaces or embodiments such as robots, virtual characters, voice assistants, and direct-manipulation interfaces.', 'participants_or_users': 'Across the included studies, 15,759 participants were reported, including general-population users, university students, experts/professionals, consumers, grade school students, and a child/caregiver pair.', 'comparison_baseline': 'Some included studies compared ChatGPT with other agents, including other AI agents, humans, or non-ChatGPT systems; the review also notes comparisons such as ChatGPT vs. robot and ChatGPT vs. human experts.', 'study_type': 'Rapid review / literature review', 'relevance_judgment': True}

{'datasets_used': 'A database of constructs and associated measurement items collected from 185 HCI-related research papers (697 constructs total), gathered from ACM SIGCHI-sponsored conferences and journals, SCIE journals, and other information science/cognitive science/psychology papers. The authors also used project descriptions entered by researchers as input to the system.', 'methods': 'System paper describing UX Remix, a web-based LLM-supported workflow for measurement item design. The authors collected and preprocessed constructs/measurement items from prior literature, stored them in a vector database (Qdrant) with embeddings, used vector search to recommend relevant constructs, and used an LLM to generate a custom construct, refine measurement items, and classify items as appropriate or inappropriate for the evaluation context.', 'key_findings': 'The paper argues that LLMs can help tailor measurement items to the current research context by leveraging prior literature, potentially improving the efficiency, reusability, rigor, and reliability of measurement item design in HCI. The authors also note that the system has not yet been validated with user studies.', 'evaluation_metrics': '', 'hci_context': 'Measurement item and construct design for UX evaluation in HCI research.', 'llm_role': 'LLM used to extract construct information from papers, preprocess/rewrite measurement items, generate custom constructs, refine measurement items for the current context, and classify items as appropriate or inappropriate.', 'participants_or_users': 'Researchers designing surveys/measurement items for HCI evaluation.', 'comparison_baseline': '', 'study_type': 'System paper / proof-of-concept system description.', 'relevance_judgment': True}

{'datasets_used': 'The paper is a review article and does not introduce a new dataset. It reports a literature collection process that initially identified 246 papers and, after expert screening, retained 78 papers. It also references datasets/corpora from surveyed works, such as a corpus and cloze evaluation for commonsense stories, STORIUM (a dataset and evaluation platform for machine-in-the-loop story generation), and other task materials like prompts, generated text, and interaction logs from interactive writing and prompt-engineering systems.', 'methods': 'Systematic review of HCI and visualization techniques for NLG/LLM-based text generation. The authors define four core terms, search relevant HCI/NLP venues using keywords such as text generation, natural language generation models, creative writing, and writing support, then screen papers with three experts. They propose a taxonomy across three levels (data, model, system) and classify works by tasks, visualization techniques, and HCI methods.', 'key_findings': 'The review concludes that HCI methods and visualization techniques improve user experience, transparency, interpretability, and control in NLG/LLM systems. At the data level they support syntactic and semantic analysis; at the model level they help explain global/local behavior and feature importance; at the system level they enable interactive generation and exploration. The paper also notes limitations such as engineering complexity, computational cost, real-time visualization challenges, and cognitive overload for non-expert users, while highlighting opportunities for broader adoption and better user feedback integration.', 'evaluation_metrics': 'The review itself does not report a unified quantitative evaluation. Across surveyed works, metrics mentioned include performance scores, response quality, evaluation of generated text, and user feedback/satisfaction metrics. The paper also discusses interpretability, usability, and user comprehension qualitatively.', 'hci_context': 'Human-computer interaction and visualization for natural language generation models, especially text generation, writing assistance, prompt engineering, story generation, summarization, interactive exploration of model outputs, and model interpretability.', 'llm_role': 'LLMs/NLG models are used as text generators, interactive writing assistants, prompt-driven conversational systems, and models whose internal behavior is visualized or interpreted. In some surveyed systems they also support iterative prompt refinement, story ideation, and human-in-the-loop generation.', 'participants_or_users': 'The review covers diverse users from the surveyed literature, including non-expert users, writers, authors, students, parents, and other end users interacting with writing assistants and prompt-based systems.', 'comparison_baseline': 'No single baseline is evaluated in this review. Across the surveyed papers, comparisons include baseline models, side-by-side model comparisons, and human or non-LLM workflows in individual studies.', 'study_type': 'Review article / survey paper', 'relevance_judgment': True}

{'datasets_used': 'A conducted dataset containing specified information from 300 CHI papers (randomly selected from 2148 CHI conference articles from 2020–2022); manually selected vectors/labels for each paper; paper text from HTML/PDF/zip/rar/7z academic documents; prompt-defined extraction targets including number of participants, recruitment method, number of tasks, type of experiment, experimental variables, and number of trials.', 'methods': 'Developed an information retrieval system for HCI empirical papers using structured text analysis plus LLMs (GPT-3.5/text-davinci-003 and Llama-2-70b). The pipeline used preprocessing, Named Entity Recognition, keyword extraction, removal of references/headers, and API-based extraction from paper text. The system was evaluated by comparing model outputs to manually annotated values for 300 CHI papers using accuracy and mean absolute error, and a random-sample baseline was also reported.', 'key_findings': 'GPT-3.5 slightly outperformed Llama-2 on extraction quality (accuracy 58% vs 56%; MAE 7.00 vs 7.63). Under a tolerance of one for numerical features, GPT-3.5 reached 62% accuracy versus Llama’s 59%. Both LLMs substantially outperformed a random baseline (13% accuracy). The paper concludes that LLMs can improve HCI data extraction efficiency and usefulness, but extraction remains challenging for ambiguous parameters and multi-stage experiments.', 'evaluation_metrics': 'Accuracy, mean absolute error (MAE), processing speed (papers/sec), latency (seconds per paper), memory consumption (MB), and a random-sample baseline accuracy; also accuracy under an approximation/tolerance of one for numerical features.', 'hci_context': 'HCI literature review and data work: extracting experimental details from CHI conference papers to support literature reviews and analysis of HCI research methods.', 'llm_role': 'Information extraction and question-answering assistant for scientific papers; the LLMs were used to extract structured experimental data from paper text and answer user questions.', 'participants_or_users': 'HCI researchers/users of the retrieval tool; the paper itself analyzes CHI papers rather than recruiting human study participants.', 'comparison_baseline': 'Randomly generated samples from a fitted normal distribution compared against actual data (13% accuracy). GPT-3.5 was also compared with Llama-2.', 'study_type': 'System paper with empirical evaluation on a curated paper dataset.', 'relevance_judgment': True}

{'datasets_used': 'User-provided story prompts (title, genre, protagonist details, brief description/world settings) from 15 participants; generated story outputs across 5 scenes per story; editable knowledge graphs created and modified during the study; Stage 1 and Stage 2 survey responses; qualitative free-text feedback/comments; paired ratings for stories with and without KG assistance.', 'methods': 'Two-stage user study using an interactive online storytelling platform with a KG-assisted LLM pipeline. Stage 1 compared two versions of each participant’s story prompt (with KG vs. without KG) under editor mode off. Stage 2 enabled editor mode, allowing participants to edit the KG after each generated scene and choose to regenerate or continue. The system used a modular KG pipeline (initialization, scene generation, update, optional edit/regeneration) and the paper analyzed results with descriptive statistics and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests on paired ratings; a post hoc kinetic vs. introspective narrative split was also applied.', 'key_findings': 'Overall KG assistance did not significantly improve story quality across all stories, though it slightly improved aggregated ratings and some criteria (notably Characters). KG benefits were strongest for kinetic/action-oriented narratives, where ratings improved significantly and participants reported better structure, pacing, characterization, and immersion. For introspective narratives, KG assistance tended to reduce ratings and could make stories feel overly literal, rigid, or bland. In Stage 2, most participants reported a strong sense of control and preferred the editing system; KG editing was described as engaging, interactive, playful, and creative, especially for concrete action-driven changes.', 'evaluation_metrics': 'Five-point Likert ratings for Theme, Setting, Structure, Plot, Pace, Consistency, Characters, Dialogue, and Holistic overall quality; aggregated criterion score across the eight criteria; standard deviation; Wilcoxon signed-rank test p-values; descriptive percentages for perceived control and preference for the editing system; qualitative thematic analysis of open-ended feedback.', 'hci_context': 'Interactive AI-assisted generative storytelling and human-AI co-creation, specifically long-form story generation with editable knowledge graphs for user control.', 'llm_role': 'Story generator and KG-assisted narrative engine; also used for KG extraction/scene generation in the pipeline, with GPT-4o additionally used as an auxiliary classifier for the post hoc kinetic/introspective labeling sanity check.', 'participants_or_users': '15 participants from diverse academic, industry, and creative backgrounds; 14 participated in Stage 2 editing.', 'comparison_baseline': 'Story generation without KG assistance (KG-free version) compared against KG-assisted generation; Stage 1 also compared editor mode off vs. editor mode on in separate conditions.', 'study_type': 'System paper with two-stage user study and mixed-method evaluation.', 'relevance_judgment': True}
